jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e106.summary: Rubric for the first question of the Prologue—whether theology is a science—with cross-references to the parallel treatments in Aquinas (ST I q.1 a.2) and Scotus's Prologue.

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e115.summary: Lays out the plan of the Prologue's questions: theology is examined first in itself according to its formal, material, and final causes (the efficient cause being uncontroversial), then in comparison with other sciences. Under the formal cause, the first issue—whether theology is a science—is split into three: theology as commonly taught; theology given a special light claimed for more perfect doctors; and whether God could communicate scientific knowledge of the articles to a wayfarer. It then opens the first objection: wisdom includes science, and theology, as knowledge of divine things, is wisdom (Augustine), so it is a science.
claims: The inquiry into theology's formal cause comprises whether it is a science and whether it is one
Since wisdom includes science and theology is wisdom, theology is a science (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e159.summary: Second objection: by elimination among Aristotle's intellectual habits in Ethics VI—theology is not opinion or suspicion (it cannot be false), nor art or prudence (it concerns God, not makeables or doables), nor understanding of self-evident principles—so it must be science or wisdom, and either way science.
claims: By sufficient division of the intellectual habits, theology must be science or wisdom (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e191.summary: Third objection: Jeremiah 9 speaks of glorying in 'knowing' God, which refers to knowledge of God through Scripture or theology; hence theology is science.
claims: Scriptural language of 'knowing' God implies theology is science (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e202.summary: First argument to the contrary: science is an intellectual virtue, but theology is not, because a virtue perfects a power toward its optimum and theology, like the faith from whose articles it proceeds, produces no clear evidence, which is the intellect's optimum.
claims: Theology is not an intellectual virtue because it yields no evidence of what it teaches

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e228.summary: Second contrary argument: the habit of principles is more perfect than the habit of conclusions; faith, the habit of theology's principles, is not listed among the intellectual virtues, so neither is theology.
claims: If faith, the habit of theology's principles, is not an intellectual virtue, neither is theology

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e246.summary: Begins the response by distinguishing three senses of 'theology'. The first is the habit by which we assent to what Scripture teaches as it is taught there. This usage is justified by analogy with natural philosophy—except that, whereas knowing what Aristotle thought is not knowing the truth where he erred, knowing the mind of the inspired authors of the canon is knowing the truth, since they never departed from it.
claims: Theology in a first sense is the habit of assenting to the contents of Scripture as taught there
Knowing the mind of Scripture's inspired authors is knowing the truth of things, unlike knowing Aristotle's opinions

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e285.summary: Second sense: theology as the habit by which the faith and the contents of Scripture are defended and declared from principles better known to us. This is Augustine's 'science' in De Trinitate XIV, by which faith is begotten, nourished, defended, and strengthened, and which many faithful lack; it is also what Lombard intends in his Prologue when he says he will 'show the faith fortified' by the authorities of the Fathers.
claims: Theology in a second sense defends and declares the faith from principles better known to us
Augustine's scientia in De Trinitate XIV and Lombard's stated aim correspond to this second sense

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e333.summary: Third sense, the most common though perhaps not the truest: theology as the habit of conclusions deduced from the articles of faith and the sayings of Scripture as from principles.
claims: Theology is commonly taken as the habit of conclusions deduced from the articles of faith

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e347.summary: Applies the first sense: theology as assent to Scripture as taught does not differ from faith, since such assent rests solely on divine authority, which belongs to faith alone. Asking whether this theology is science is asking whether faith is science, which no one doubts it is not, except in Augustine's very broad sense of knowing by testimony; so this sense is set aside.
claims: Theology in the first sense is identical with faith
Faith is not formally science except in the broadest sense

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e382.summary: Applies the second sense: faith and defensive theology concern the same things, faith by authority and theology by reason, so the question becomes whether faith and science can coexist about the same object.
claims: The question about defensive theology reduces to whether faith and science can coexist about the same thing
concepts: faith and science of the same object

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e400.summary: Applies the third sense: asking whether deductive theology is science is asking whether anything truly known can be demonstratively concluded from the articles of faith.
claims: The question about deductive theology reduces to whether articles of faith can ground demonstrations

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e416.summary: Announces that the question will be treated in the last two senses (faith and science about the same object; scientific deduction from articles), but first rebuts objections to the threefold distinction. First objection against the first member: faith assents only to what is revealed, not to what is deduced, yet Scripture contains deductions—e.g. Paul in 1 Cor 15 concludes our resurrection from Christ's—so not everything in Scripture is held by faith alone.
claims: The question will be pursued in the second and third senses of theology
Objection: Scripture contains deductions, so its contents are not held by faith alone

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e464.summary: Second objection against the first member: faith is infused, but the habit of knowing Scripture's contents is acquired by study, so theology in the first sense is not the same as faith.
claims: Objection: the habit of knowing Scripture is acquired, faith is infused, so they differ

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e477.summary: Objection against the second member: the habit that defends and declares Scripture stands to Scripture as an opinative habit stands to geometry or natural science; just as such probable opinion does not make a second geometry, the defensive habit is not a second theology but is merely annexed to theology properly so called.
claims: Objection: the defensive habit is annexed to theology, not a distinct theology, as opinion is annexed to a science

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e515.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith assents to what is revealed and not to what is merely humanly deduced, but scriptural deductions are themselves held as divinely inspired—otherwise one could deny the inference and falsify Scripture—and many deduced items are elsewhere revealed absolutely (our resurrection in Job 19, Daniel 12, the Gospels). So all such content is held solely or principally by faith.
claims: Deductions contained in Scripture are held as divinely inspired, not as humanly reasoned
Denying a scriptural inference would falsify Scripture
Much of what Scripture deduces it also reveals absolutely

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e559.summary: Reply to the second objection: a habit can act only on a presented object, so the articles must be proposed to us through study of Scripture; the resulting acquired habit only presents the object and does not by itself cause assent—believers and unbelievers alike can know what Scripture says—while assent comes from faith that Scripture is inspired. This acquired habit is therefore not what is meant by theology in the first sense, which remains identical with faith.
claims: The acquired knowledge of Scripture's contents merely presents the object and does not cause assent
Assent to Scripture comes solely or principally from faith that it is inspired
Theology in the first sense does not differ from faith

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e614.summary: Reply to the objection against the second member: to call the defensive habit 'annexed' yet not distinct is contradictory, since nothing is annexed to itself; and the objectors also contradict their own doctrine elsewhere that opinion cannot coexist with science, while here they make an opinative habit annexed to science of the same objects.
claims: What is annexed to a habit is distinct from it
The objectors contradict their own claim that opinion and science are incompatible

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e656.summary: Further reply: the geometry analogy fails. Geometrical science appropriates the name 'geometry' by its superior certainty, but no theological habit is science properly speaking, so the name 'theology' is appropriated to none and belongs to all assent-producing theological habits, especially the defensive habit, as Augustine attests. The objections to the distinction therefore fail.
claims: No theological habit is science in the proper sense
The name 'theology' belongs to all assent-producing theological habits, chiefly the defensive one

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e693.summary: Opens the first article: whether faith and science can be in the same person about the same conclusion. Distinguishes faith resting on human authority, which is merely a very weak opinion since the topical argument from human authority is the weakest, from faith resting on divine authority. The first is treated first, as the question of opinion and science.
claims: Faith resting on human authority is a very weak form of opinion
The coexistence question is first treated for human faith, then for divine faith

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e726.summary: Gives the first way of distinguishing science from opinion, by their conclusions: science concerns a necessary conclusion known to be unable to be otherwise (Posterior Analytics I); opinion concerns a conclusion that is, or is judged by the opiner to be, contingent—true opinion if it is actually contingent, false opinion if only judged so.
claims: On the conclusion-based distinction, science is of necessary conclusions and opinion of conclusions judged contingent

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e771.summary: Shows that on the conclusion-based distinction, science and opinion of the same conclusion cannot coexist in act: judging that the same conclusion both cannot and can be otherwise is judging contradictories true together, which is impossible (Metaphysics IV); this is Aristotle's sense at the end of Posterior Analytics I.
claims: Acts of knowing and opining the same conclusion, distinguished by conclusion, are incompatible

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e813.summary: Extends the result to habits: habits caused by formally incompatible acts are incompatible, since every act generating one corrupts the other (Ethics II). Hence science and opinion so understood, and therefore science and faith based on human authority, cannot coexist.
claims: Habits caused by formally incompatible acts are incompatible
Science and faith based on human authority cannot coexist under the conclusion-based distinction

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e842.summary: Proposes a second, more proper way of distinguishing science and opinion: by their middle terms. While similar habits (science from science) are distinguished by object, dissimilar habits about the same object, like science and opinion, must be distinguished by middle—necessary and evidently so for science, contingent or judged contingent for opinion. Even opponents implicitly accept this by positing an opinative habit for every science. On this view science and opinion can coexist about the same conclusion, in act or at least in habit.
claims: Dissimilar habits about the same object are distinguished by their middles, not their conclusions
Science proceeds through an evidently necessary middle, opinion through a contingent one
So distinguished, science and opinion can coexist about the same conclusion

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e903.summary: Turning to acts: if knowing and opining are really distinct acts, they cannot coexist, because by the course of nature an intellect cannot have several acts of understanding at once (as proved elsewhere); thus no one can simultaneously know and opine the same or different things.
claims: Several acts of understanding cannot exist simultaneously in one intellect by the course of nature

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e929.summary: Counterfactually supposing several simultaneous acts possible: one could know and opine the same conclusion when opining through a contingent middle mistakenly judged necessary, since both acts then judge the conclusion necessary and are conformable; such assent is opinion, not science, because the middle is in fact contingent, and opinion admits deception.
claims: If simultaneous acts were possible, opining through a middle mistakenly judged necessary could coexist with knowing the same conclusion
Assent through a contingent middle judged necessary is opinion

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e988.summary: Answers the objection that such opining involves deception, which opposes knowing: knowing and being deceived about different things are compatible, and here the deception concerns only the middle, not the conclusion, which the opiner rightly judges necessary.
claims: Knowing and being deceived are compatible when they concern different objects
The opiner's error concerns the middle, not the conclusion

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1031.summary: But if the opiner judges the middle contingent, opining cannot coexist with knowing even granting simultaneous acts, because one cannot know a conclusion with certainty and fear (formido) about it at once; assent solely through a middle judged able to fail is with fear. The same holds of belief based on human authority, which is opinion.
claims: Opinion through a middle judged contingent is assent with fear and cannot coexist with certain knowledge
Belief on human authority is a form of such opinion

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1092.summary: States the rule for habits: habits caused by formally compatible acts can coexist, those caused by formally incompatible acts (acts bearing opposed relations to the same object) cannot. Acts not so opposed generate compatible habits, though Durandus holds that in fact several acts of understanding never occur together naturally; the previous two conclusions were drawn on the opposite supposition.
claims: Compatibility of habits follows the formal compatibility of their generating acts
Acts are formally incompatible when they include opposed relations to the same object

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1136.summary: Reframes the question given that knowing and opining as distinct acts cannot coexist: the real question is whether a contingent middle (apt to cause opinion) and a necessary middle (apt to cause science) can concur in causing one and the same assent to the same conclusion.
claims: The coexistence of science and opinion must be understood as the concurrence of necessary and contingent middles in one assent

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1165.summary: First answer: a contingent middle judged necessary can concur with a truly necessary middle to cause one assent, because assent depends entirely on how the middles are judged by the reasoner, not on their nature in itself; and two necessary middles can be combined in a single demonstration to produce one assent.
claims: A contingent middle judged necessary can concur with a necessary middle in one assent
Assent to a conclusion depends on the reasoner's estimation of the middles, not their nature in itself

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1213.summary: Second answer: even a middle judged contingent—drawn from appearances or human authority—can concur with a necessary middle in one assent. One who has an evident necessary middle does not need authority or probable arguments (necessity is excluded), but their compossibility is not excluded.
claims: A necessary middle excludes the need for, but not the compossibility of, authority or probable middles

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1248.summary: Argues for compossibility: the only conceivable obstacle to such concurrence is the opposition between evident and inevident, certain and doubtful assent; it remains to show that this does not prevent concurrence.
claims: The only obstacle to concurrence is the opposition of evident and inevident, certain and doubtful

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1286.summary: Illustrates with the sun and a star: separately they cause bright and dim light, incompatible conditions, yet when together they concur as partial causes forming one total cause of a single light, with brightness appropriated to the sun because of its superior power, though the star contributes imperceptibly.
claims: Causes that separately produce incompatible conditions can concur as partial causes in one common effect
The effect's perfection is appropriated to the more perfect partial cause

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1349.summary: Explains why such concurrence is possible: bright and dim here are not habit and privation in a common subject (as light and darkness, whose causes cannot concur) but degrees of perfection within light, not really distinct from it, arising only from the perfection or imperfection of the cause; joined to a more perfect cause, the imperfect one no longer yields an imperfect effect.
claims: Clarity and obscurity are degrees of perfection, not habit and privation
Causes of degrees of perfection can concur, whereas causes of a habit and its privation cannot

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1391.summary: Applies the analogy to cognition: all knowledge of truth is a light (Eph. 3), and clarity and obscurity in cognition are degrees of perfection deriving from the middle, not privations. Authority alone yields obscure, inevident cognition and a necessary middle alone clear, evident cognition; joined, they produce one clear and evident cognition as partial causes of one total cause, the evidence being attributed chiefly to the necessary middle.
claims: Cognition is a spiritual light whose clarity is a degree of perfection derived from the middle
Authority and a necessary middle can jointly cause one clear and evident cognition
The evidence of such cognition is chiefly attributed to the necessary middle

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1472.summary: Extends the result to certainty and doubt: contingent middles and human authority alone cause doubtful assent, a necessary middle certain assent, and these two assents cannot coexist; yet the middles can concur in one assent that is only certain. So science, opinion, and faith based on human authority can coexist about the same object—not as distinct habits with distinct acts, but because their middles concur in one assent.
claims: Doubtful and certain assent to the same conclusion cannot coexist
Necessary and probable middles can concur in one certain assent
Science, opinion, and human faith coexist only as concurring middles of one assent, not as distinct acts

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1529.summary: Notes agreement with the common doctrine, citing Aquinas (ST I-II q.67 a.3; III q.9 a.3 ad 2) that one can know the same conclusion through probable and demonstrative middles and that opinion can coexist with demonstrative science—possible not by plurality of acts but in the manner just explained.
claims: The conclusion agrees with Aquinas's teaching that opinion can coexist with demonstrative science

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1551.summary: Turns to faith resting on divine authority. As to habits, infused faith can coexist with science of the same object: faith extends to all revealed truths, and some revealed truths not deduced from others—such as that God is one (Deut. 6)—are known by many faithful through acquired demonstration.
claims: The infused habit of faith can coexist with demonstrative science of the same truth
That God is one is both revealed and demonstrable

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1594.summary: As to acts: for revealed truths demonstrable to wayfarers (e.g. that God is one), divine authority and demonstration can concur in one assent, as argued above; it would be harsh to say a believer who acquires such science no longer believes God is one on God's word. But articles like the Trinity and the Incarnation are not demonstrable by the common course, so wayfarers have faith but not science of them—not because of the evident/inevident opposition, already removed, but because of the indemonstrable nature of the matter. Three points will show this.
claims: For demonstrable revealed truths, faith and science concur in a single assent
Articles such as Trinity and Incarnation cannot be known scientifically by wayfarers in the common course
The obstacle is the indemonstrability of the matter, not an opposition of evident and inevident

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1649.summary: First point: the articles cannot be demonstrated to be so. Not a priori, since their cause (where they have one, as the Incarnation) is the hidden divine will and the Trinity has no cause; not a posteriori, since all effects proceed from God according to what is common to the three persons (knowledge, power, will) and so lead only to the unity of essence and essential attributes—and all articles somehow include the Trinity. Moreover, demonstration compels assent, but assent to the articles is free (Augustine), else pagan philosophers would be compelled.
claims: Articles of faith cannot be demonstrated a priori or a posteriori
Creaturely effects reveal only what is common to the divine persons
Assent to the articles is free, whereas demonstration compels assent

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1727.summary: Second point: it cannot be demonstrated that the articles involve no impossibility. Such a demonstration would have to argue from creatures, which rather suggest impossibility (in creatures supposits are distinguished by absolutes, and a complete substantial nature constitutes its own supposit). Moreover, whatever is intrinsic to God is necessary, so demonstrating the possibility of the Trinity would demonstrate its actuality, which is impossible. Finally, such demonstration would remove the difficulty and thus the merit of faith.
claims: The possibility of the articles cannot be demonstrated
Creaturely evidence rather suggests the impossibility of Trinity and Incarnation
In God, possibility and actuality of intrinsic features coincide, so demonstrating possibility would demonstrate the article
Demonstrating the articles' possibility would remove the merit of faith

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1792.summary: Third point: not all arguments against the articles can be resolved scientifically. Arguments faulty in form can be refuted by logic (the art of the Elenchi), but those faulty in matter—e.g. 'distinct supposits always have distinct natures'—can be answered only by denying a premise whose falsity holds only in the divine case, and the falsity of that premise is known in the same way as the truth of its negation, namely only by faith.
claims: Arguments against the articles that fail in form can be scientifically refuted
Arguments failing in matter can be answered only by premises known by faith

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1849.summary: Concludes that, regarding faith's special indemonstrable matter, faith and science do not coexist in the same person about the same articles in the common course by which theology is had: neither the articles, nor their possibility, can be demonstrated, nor can objections be clearly resolved.
claims: Faith and science do not coexist regarding the articles for wayfarers in the common course

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1873.summary: Explains the qualifier 'in the common course' by two views: some hold that a wayfarer could miraculously have abstractive science of God as one and three (to be examined later); others hold that the Apostles and witnesses of Christ's miracles had true science of his divinity, since it is self-evident that God cannot lie, so whoever knows God testifies to something knows it.
claims: Some posit miraculous abstractive science of the Trinity in a wayfarer
Some hold that witnesses of Christ's miracles had science of his divinity

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1907.summary: Presents the second view's account: God's testimony could be self-evident either to the blessed seeing God move someone's intellect, or to a wayfarer seeing an effect exceeding all created power performed as testimony—so the Apostles, seeing Lazarus raised, knew God testified to Christ's divinity and thus had science of Christ's divinity and of his doctrine's truth.
claims: According to some, miracles performed as divine testimony yield scientific knowledge of what is testified
According to some, the Apostles had science of Christ's divinity from his miracles

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e1949.summary: Rejects that account for wayfarers on three grounds: demonstration compels assent, yet many who saw Christ's miracles did not believe (John 11, 15); if the Apostles had science they would have lost the merit of believing (Gregory); and even granting that an effect could only be God's, it is not self-evident that it is done to confirm what a given speaker says, since no man is self-evidently incapable of error or deceit.
claims: Miracles did not compel assent, so they were not demonstrations of Christ's divinity
Scientific knowledge of Christ's divinity would remove the merit of the Apostles' faith
It is not self-evident that a miracle is performed to confirm a particular speaker's claim

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2023.summary: Answers the rejoinder that God would bear witness to falsehood if he worked a miracle upon Christ's invocation were Christ not God: even if a miracle follows an invocation, it is not self-evident that it is done because of the invocation, since a prophet may foreknow a divine act by revelation and falsely attribute its purpose. Durandus concludes the Apostles had no science properly speaking of Christ's divinity, though a more perfect notitia than ours, and that theology as the habit declaring and defending the articles is not science properly and simply speaking.
claims: A miracle's coincidence with an invocation does not make self-evident that it confirms the invocation
The Apostles lacked science of Christ's divinity but had a more perfect knowledge than ours
Defensive theology is not science properly and simply speaking

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2104.summary: Opens the second article: whether theology as the habit of conclusions deduced from the articles is properly science. Durandus doubts this sense is accurate, arguing that what is supposedly deduced from the articles—e.g. that divine persons are distinguished by relations, or that Christ had real flesh—is rather adduced to sustain or declare the article (showing its possibility, clarifying its meaning), as Christ did in Luke 24. Practical deductions, however, abound in moral and homiletic works.
claims: Supposed deductions from the articles are better understood as adduced to sustain or declare them
The relational distinction of divine persons is posited to defend the possibility of the Trinity
Christ's real flesh is adduced to clarify the article of his humanity and resurrection
Practical consequences are genuinely deduced from the articles in moral theology

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2200.summary: Argues that in either case theology as a deductive habit is not properly science: demonstration proceeds from necessary premises that are self-evident or reducible to self-evident ones (Posterior Analytics I), but the articles of faith are neither, being held on the authority of Scripture, whose inspiration is itself not self-evident.
claims: Demonstration requires premises self-evident or reducible to the self-evident
The articles are not self-evident nor reducible to self-evident truths
That Scripture is inspired is not self-evident
Theology as deductive habit is not properly science

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2244.summary: First objection to this argument (the subalternation strategy): the major holds only for non-subalternate sciences, since a subalternate science's principles are neither self-evident nor concluded within it but merely believed from the subalternating science.
claims: Objection: subalternate sciences proceed from principles merely believed

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2284.summary: Second objection: theology does not proceed only from believed articles but joins to them self-evident premises, by virtue of which the conclusion can be known.
claims: Objection: combining an article with a self-evident premise yields a known conclusion

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2300.summary: Reply to the subalternation objection: principles merely believed on another's authority cannot ground science, since principles must be more evident than conclusions. Subalternate sciences make their principles evident (quia est) through sense, memory, and experience as described in Metaphysics I.
claims: Principles believed solely on authority cannot ground science
Subalternate sciences make their principles evident through sense, memory, and experience

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2329.summary: Reply to the second objection: just as a necessary and a contingent premise yield only a contingent conclusion, so an evident and an inevident premise yield no evident conclusion, since the conclusion's connection cannot be more necessary or known than the middle's connection with each extreme. Deductive theology is science only broadly, as concluding from truths unmanifest to the reasoner; this agrees with the common view that a science not reducible to naturally known principles is not univocally science.
claims: The conclusion follows the weaker premise in evidence as in modality
Deductive theology is science only in a broad sense
A science not reducible to naturally known principles is not univocally a science

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2384.summary: Reply to the first initial argument: Aristotle's wisdom includes science because of its mode of proceeding; theology may be called wisdom by reason of its subject (Augustine's sense), but it falls short of science's mode of proceeding.
claims: Theology is wisdom by its subject but not science in its mode of proceeding

jsnvu6-d1e88-d1e2406.summary: Replies to the remaining initial arguments: Aristotle knew nothing of cognition through divine authority, so theology falls under none of his intellectual habits; and Jeremiah's 'knowing' is the broad knowledge of divine things given by Scripture as revealed, not Aristotelian scientia. The contrary arguments, proving theology is not strictly science, are conceded.
claims: Theology falls outside Aristotle's classification of intellectual habits
Scriptural 'scire' is not Aristotelian scientia
Theology is not properly and strictly a science

jsnvu6-d1e88.summary: Question 1 of the Prologue asks whether theology, as commonly taught, is properly a science. Durandus distinguishes three senses of theology: (1) assent to Scripture as taught there, which is simply identical with faith; (2) the habit defending and declaring faith from better-known principles (Augustine's scientia, Lombard's project); and (3) the habit deducing conclusions from the articles. After rebutting objections to this distinction, he treats the second sense as the question whether faith and science can coexist about the same object. Distinguishing science and opinion by their middles rather than their conclusions, and denying that several intellectual acts can be simultaneous, he argues—using the sun-and-star analogy of partial causes—that necessary and probable middles (or authority) can concur in one certain, evident assent; thus faith and science can coexist regarding demonstrable revealed truths such as God's unity. But the articles proper (Trinity, Incarnation) cannot be demonstrated, nor their possibility shown, nor all objections scientifically resolved; even the Apostles' witness of miracles gave no proper science of Christ's divinity. Regarding the third sense, he doubts that theology really deduces from the articles (rather it adduces to sustain and declare them) and argues that, since the articles are not self-evident, conclusions drawn from them—even with evident premises added, and despite the appeal to subalternation—are not science properly but only broadly. Theology is wisdom by its subject but not strictly a science.
claims: Theology taken as assent to Scripture is identical with faith
Science and opinion are properly distinguished by their middles, and necessary and probable middles can concur in one assent
Faith and science can coexist about revealed truths that are demonstrable, such as God's unity
The articles of faith, their possibility, and the solutions to all objections against them cannot be demonstrated to a wayfarer in the common course
Theology, whether as defensive or deductive habit, is not a science properly and strictly so called
Subalternation cannot rescue theology's scientific status because principles held on authority alone do not ground science
